concept.name: Institutional investor
concept.definition: An institutional investor is an organization that pools or manages large amounts of money and trades securities on behalf of others or of the institution — for example banks, insurance companies, registered investment companies, investment advisers, pension and employee benefit plans, and government entities. FINRA Rule 2210(a)(4) enumerates such persons (including persons described in Rule 4512(c)) as 'institutional investors' for communications purposes.
concept.intuition: Institutional investors are the 'whales' of the market: pension funds, mutual funds, insurers, and endowments trading in large blocks with professional staff, in contrast to individuals trading their own savings.
concept.mechanics: Institutions trade through prime brokers and execution brokers, often splitting large parent orders into child orders via algorithms to control market impact. Their size gives them access to block trading, dark pools, and negotiated liquidity, but also means their orders can move prices, so execution strategy and information leakage are central concerns.
concept.failure_modes: Large institutional orders create market impact and information leakage, and crowded institutional positioning can amplify drawdowns when many institutions unwind similar trades. Agency problems arise because institutions trade other people's money.
concept.misconceptions: Institutional investors are not uniformly 'smart money' with superior returns; much institutional flow is index-tracking or liability-driven. Nor does institutional participation guarantee market stability — herding among institutions can be destabilizing.
concept.example: A pension fund must invest a $200 million contribution; its trader works the order over several days through an execution algorithm to avoid driving up the price of the stocks it buys.
